title: Learning by listening and developing his own style
summary: Turetsky and Garland discuss learning from records and watching older players (Willie Ruff's conservatory without walls); Garland refuses to imitate anyone.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Oh, yes. Right. And you're still doing it, and that's great. We've heard some of the recent stuff, though. It's fine. Basically, that's the way most of, I think, your contemporaries, or your friends learned, by listening to people who played well.
That's what I did.
And studying them. I think the kids growing up in the last 20 years listened to records more, you know.
That's right.
So they listened to different people play.
And those guys over in Germany do the same thing.
That's right. That's right.
They get those records and they play it just right off the record.
Right. Yeah. Yeah. Remember Johnny Windhurst and Eddie Hubble and those guys would take Louis Armstrong's -- the Hot Five things and learn all those solos.
All them solos.
Was it Bob Wilber, the soprano saxophone player, that knew all the Sidney Bechet solos.
Yeah. That's right.
Yeah. I mean, that's a way. That's one way. I guess Barry Martin got into music by listening to these records and things.
He used to follow the bands all around and come all the way down to New Orleans.
Sure.
Get on a boat, he'd get on a ship, you know, and he'd come down to New Orleans, and he'd come back and stay in New Orleans. That's where he learned all his drumming.

Right. That's the way you really do learn it. Willie Ruff. Willie Ruff is a professor, Tootie, at Yale University, and he's a bass player and he's a french horn player and he plays jazz and he plays classical music, and he's brought a big jazz program to Yale, and he says that musicians like you, artists like you, got educated in the conservatory without walls. In other words, in the real world. You heard Henry Kimball, Sr., play. And you heard Nicholson play. And after that, you developed your own style and many people have come to hear you play and see what they can learn. And we grow that way, you know. I didn't -- wasn't in this
part of the country, but I did hear Pops play and I did hear Slow Drag play, and Walter Page, and so on.
Yeah.
And so I listened to your recordings and other people's recordings, and I learned something. And that's a nice way to learn, you know?
That's right.
Sharing all these ideas and getting together. That's a lovely way to do it. But, oh, let's get back to our story.
I tried to -- I wouldn't try to imitate nobody else. I wanted my own style.
Right.
I developed my own style. And then I had them same guys I was watching come to me.
Right.
I developed my own style and still got my own style.
